thread.title: Apple: Is the HomePod a Bust?

title: Apple: Is the HomePod a Bust?
text:
David Marino-Nachison April 12, 2018 1:57 p.m. ET 
When Apple’s HomePod smart speaker hit shelves in February, a theme kept bubbling up : the notion that, while it sounded great, its tech needed work, and it wasn’t essential, particularly at the price. 
Now, it seems, the marketplace is backing that thesis up. This week, Bloomberg reported that Apple (AAPL), a Barron’s Next 50 stock, has scaled back its sales forecasts for the device as its market share has slipped. Other analysts and research groups have recently reported similar concepts. Newsletter Sign-up 
March numbers from Slice Intelligence reported a strong debut fotr the HomePod but put its share below 1%, well below that of a number of Amazon.com (AMZN) devices, among others. At a time when the smart speaker market is growing quickly , investors might’ve expected a warmer reception. 
There might be reasons to temper the negativity. While it’s surely bad news that the HomePod wasn’t available during last year’s holiday season, when Amazon, Alphabet ’s (GOOGL) Google and others used discounting to sell loads of their devices, this time it will be. 
The company will have time to issue software updates, contemplate its own discounts, and perhaps even produce a new, smaller, cheaper device in time for this winter. Many of the kinks, you might say, could be ironed out, leaving more reasons to buy something on which to listen to The Kinks , you might say. 
And stories about the HomePod leaving weird rings on furniture have seemingly stopped being published. 
Slice data suggested that the kind of person who bought the HomePod was often what might be called an Apple “fanboy”—males who were already sufficiently big fans of the company that they also bought the iPhone X, and may have held out on other smart speaker buys to wait for Apple’s. Illustration: Slice Intelligence 
Maybe that’s a good thing. As Guggenheim analysts noted in February, products like the HomePod give it more ways to get money from its “loyal, high-value customers” and more doorways through which to try to pull services revenue . 
But it arguably runs counter to some of the broader logic around smart speakers these days, with big companies racing to get them into as many homes as possible, giving them a peek at the potential of smart home technology. 
Amazon’s Echo, particularly, introduced millions to a category of product most probably didn’t even realize they wanted before it existed—and helped digital assistant Alexa rival or even surpass, in the cultural consciousness sense, Siri. 
HomePod flop or not, that‘s seems like a fight Apple needs to be in.
